title: The withered hand (Mark 3:1–6)
hook: he looks around in anger at hard hearts, and heals on the sabbath anyway

segments.voice: Yesterday, hungry friends in a grain field, and the sabbath defended as a gift. Your line was made for people. Did a rest actually heal you a little? Day one hundred sixty-seven.

A meeting where everyone is waiting to see which side someone will take: that's the mood in this synagogue, on a sabbath. Jesus walks in, and there's a man whose hand is withered, shrunken and useless. And Mark says some people there are watching Jesus, not the man. Watching to see whether he'll heal on the sabbath, so they'll have something against him. The man with the hand has become a test case. Jesus knows it. The whole room knows it. And Mark tells us what Jesus felt. Today: the withered hand.
screen: `A ROOM THAT'S WATCHING.` → `A MAN WITH A WITHERED HAND.` → `A TEST CASE.`

segments.voice: Jesus doesn't do it quietly in a corner. He tells the man, stand up in the middle. Then he turns to the room with a question, in the old King James Bible: "Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill?" It's a question with only one decent answer. "But they held their peace." Nobody speaks. And then comes the verse Mark keeps and the other gospels soften: "when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand." Anger and grief, in the same breath. Mark names what grieves him: the hardness of their hearts. Hardness here is a word for skin that's gone thick and stiff, like a callus. A heart that can't feel anymore. Then the man stretches out his hand, and it's restored, whole as the other. Notice that Jesus doesn't touch him. He just asks him to do the one thing his hand couldn't: reach. And the ending is dark. Some Pharisees go out and start planning with supporters of King Herod how to destroy Jesus. Three chapters in, and already there is a plot. Readers take a few things from this. That doing good is never out of season. That Jesus's anger is real, and aimed at hard hearts, not at hurting people. And that sometimes the healing starts when someone asks you to stretch toward what you think you can't do.
screen: `STAND UP IN THE MIDDLE.` · `TO SAVE LIFE, OR TO KILL?` · `ANGER AND GRIEF AT HARD HEARTS.` · `STRETCH FORTH THINE HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do good even if it's awkward. Settle, and breathe. Hold one hand out in front of you, palm open, and leave it there a moment. Feel the small effort of reaching. Now think of a good thing you've been putting off because it would be awkward. Thanking someone out loud. Speaking up in a meeting for someone who's being talked over. Checking on a person after a hard conversation. Picture yourself doing it, awkwardness and all. If you pray, you can open your hand to God as you do. Then let the hand rest. The bell holds the time.
Hardness, the callused heart Jesus grieved over in the watching room, right before he told the man to stretch out his hand.
Your line: stretch out your hand. Today, do the good thing that feels awkward, in the middle of the room if you have to. Day one hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Christians read this passage as a call to do good without waiting for the convenient moment, and churches often hold healing services or pray for the sick with hands outstretched or laid on them.

fork.setup: you're Jesus. a room is watching to see if you'll heal a man on the sabbath so they can accuse you. what do you do?
options: wait until tomorrow and heal him then.
call him into the middle and heal him now.

fork.reveal: he calls the man to stand in the middle, asks whether it's lawful to do good or evil, and heals him in front of everyone.

original.note: Greek: a hardening, like a callus. Mark's word for the hardness of their hearts.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle story about a hand.
what it means: a man becomes a test case, and Jesus, angry and grieved at hard hearts, heals him anyway in the middle of the room.
what a scholar hears: porosis, a callus, a hardening. and Mark alone keeps the anger, which the other gospels soften or leave out.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'You know the feeling'; the narrator's own verdict on the watchers ('rather win an argument than see a man healed') replaced by Mark's words, to avoid using the Pharisees as a foil; 'the first plot' superlative cut; practice example changed so it doesn't repeat day 159's 'apologizing'.
Claim that Mark alone mentions Jesus's anger (Matthew 12 and Luke 6 omit it); confirm.
πώρωσις: 'hardening', related to πῶρος (a callus or kind of stone). Confirm the note.
3:6: 'the Pharisees ... took counsel with the Herodians'. Phrased as 'some Pharisees' and 'supporters of King Herod' to avoid blanket framing; confirm.
Practice invites outstretching a hand; confirm it fits.
